_meta.note: Hand-written fixture. Exercises all five v0.1 signals, including one missed question and one rambling stretch.

speaker: interviewer
text: Alright, I think we're both on. Can you hear me okay?

speaker: candidate
text: Yeah, coming through fine.

speaker: interviewer
text: Great. So today I'd like you to design a URL shortener. Something like bit.ly. Take a minute if you want to think, and just talk me through your approach.

speaker: candidate
text: Sure. Before I start designing, can I ask a few questions about scope?

speaker: interviewer
text: Please do.

speaker: candidate
text: First, what kind of scale are we talking about? Is this an internal tool or something public facing?

speaker: interviewer
text: Let's say public. Assume a hundred million new URLs a month.

speaker: candidate
text: Okay. And what's the read to write ratio? For a shortener I'd guess reads dominate heavily.

speaker: interviewer
text: That's right, assume about a hundred to one.

speaker: candidate
text: Got it. Do users need custom aliases, like choosing their own short code?

speaker: interviewer
text: Let's support that, yes.

speaker: candidate
text: And do links expire?

speaker: interviewer
text: Optional expiry. Let's say the user can set a TTL if they want one.

speaker: candidate
text: Okay, one more. Do we need analytics, like click counts per link?

speaker: interviewer
text: Let's call that a nice to have. Focus on the core path first.

speaker: candidate
text: Perfect. So to summarize the requirements: shorten a long URL to a short code, redirect on lookup, optional custom alias, optional TTL, read heavy at roughly a hundred to one, a hundred million writes a month. Non-functionally I'd say redirect latency is the thing that matters most, and availability on the read path matters more than on the write path. If shortening is down for a minute that's annoying. If redirects are down, every link anyone ever made is broken.

speaker: interviewer
text: That's a good distinction. Go ahead and start on the design.

speaker: candidate
text: Let me do a quick estimate first. A hundred million writes a month is roughly forty writes a second. At a hundred to one that's four thousand reads a second. That's not enormous. Storage, if each record is around five hundred bytes, a hundred million a month is fifty gigabytes a month, so around six hundred gigs a year. Also not enormous, but it grows forever unless we expire things.

speaker: interviewer
text: Sounds reasonable. What does the architecture look like?

speaker: candidate
text: I'll start simple. A write service that takes a long URL and returns a short code. A read service that takes a short code and issues a 301 or 302 redirect. Both sit behind a load balancer. A datastore holding the mapping. And a cache in front of the read path, since reads dominate and the access pattern is very skewed, a small number of links get most of the traffic.

speaker: interviewer
text: Why 301 versus 302?

speaker: candidate
text: So the redirect is the core of the read path, and what I'd want is for it to be as fast as possible, which is why I'd put a cache in front. The cache would be Redis, probably, and I'd size it based on the working set. If we assume the top one percent of links drive most traffic, that's a manageable amount of memory. I'd also think about putting a CDN in front of that, since redirects are a great fit for edge caching, and that would cut latency for users far from the origin region quite a lot.

speaker: interviewer
text: Okay. Let's talk about how you generate the short code.

speaker: candidate
text: A few options. One, hash the long URL, take the first seven characters, base62 encode. Simple and stateless, but you get collisions and you have to handle them. Two, a counter, base62 encoded. No collisions, but a global counter is a bottleneck and the codes are sequential and guessable. Three, pre-generate a pool of random codes and hand them out from a key generation service.

speaker: interviewer
text: Which would you pick?

speaker: candidate
text: I'd go with the third, the key generation service, but let me say why rather than just picking it. The hash approach is the simplest to build but collision handling makes the write path do a read first, check if it exists, retry, and that gets worse as the table fills. The counter avoids collisions entirely and is very cheap, but sequential codes let anyone enumerate every link in the system, which is a real problem if people shorten anything private. You can fix that by range-allocating the counter across servers so it isn't globally sequential, which also fixes the bottleneck, so honestly the counter with ranged allocation is close. The pre-generated pool wins for me because the write path becomes a single fast pop from a pool, and the codes are unguessable by construction. The cost is an extra service and you have to make sure a code is never handed out twice, so the pool needs to be transactional.

speaker: interviewer
text: Good. What about storage, what would you use?

speaker: candidate
text: The access pattern is a key value lookup on short code. No joins, no complex queries. So I'd use a key value store rather than a relational database. Something like DynamoDB or Cassandra. Short code is the partition key, and the value is the long URL plus metadata, creation time, TTL, owner.

speaker: interviewer
text: You mentioned the access pattern is skewed. What happens if one link goes viral and you get a hot partition?

speaker: candidate
text: Right, so for scaling the storage layer I'd shard by short code. Since the code is effectively random in the pre-generated approach, the distribution across shards is pretty even. I'd add read replicas so the read path can fan out across them, and the write path goes to the primary. And then as the dataset grows you can add shards. The nice thing about sharding on a random key is that you don't get the hotspotting you'd get with something like a timestamp prefix, which is a classic problem in time series schemas where everything lands on the newest shard.

speaker: interviewer
text: Mm. Let's come back to that. What happens when a link expires?

speaker: candidate
text: Two parts. Lazy deletion on read, so if a lookup finds an expired record it returns a 404 and doesn't serve the redirect. And a background cleanup job that sweeps expired records so storage doesn't grow forever. The lazy check is what guarantees correctness, the sweep is just housekeeping. I'd also need to invalidate the cache entry, otherwise a cached redirect keeps serving after expiry.

speaker: interviewer
text: Good. Earlier I asked what happens with a hot partition when a link goes viral, and I don't think we covered it.

speaker: candidate
text: Ah, you're right, I answered a different question. So a single viral link means one short code, one partition, taking enormous read traffic. Sharding doesn't help because it's a single key. The cache absorbs most of it, since that one key will be resident and hot. Below that, if the cache node itself becomes the bottleneck, I'd replicate that key across cache nodes and pick one at random on read. And the CDN is really the right answer, because a viral link is exactly the case the edge handles best. The storage layer barely sees the traffic at all after that.

speaker: interviewer
text: That's better. We've got about five minutes. Anything you'd flag as a risk in this design?

speaker: candidate
text: The biggest one is the key generation service becoming a single point of failure on the write path. If it's down, nobody can create links. I'd mitigate with a local buffer of codes on each write server, so a brief outage is invisible. Second risk is cache invalidation on custom alias updates, if we let people repoint an alias. Third, I glossed over abuse. A public shortener is a phishing vector, and you'd want some scanning of target URLs and rate limiting per account. That's not really a scaling concern but it would matter in production.

speaker: interviewer
text: Good. Let's stop there. That was solid.
